articles.title_orig: Musk Can Wall Off Shanghai. He Cannot Wall Off China’s Supply Chain.
articles.title_zh: Musk Can Wall Off Shanghai. He Cannot Wall Off China’s Supply Chain.
articles.content_orig:
Despite previously dismissing a potential spinoff of Tesla’s China business, Elon Musk confirmed on October 20 that Tesla and SpaceX have each formed special committees of independent directors to evaluate a merger. Given mounting U.S.-China tensions, a combined entity valued at roughly $3.5 trillion could put that separation back on the table.
Most commentary has fixed on two hurdles: winning half of all outstanding Tesla shares, and deciding what to do with Giga Shanghai, which builds more than half of the cars Tesla sells worldwide . The working assumption is that once the China question is “solved” through a spin-off, a sale or a firewall, the combined company can become a clean, defense-grade American champion.
That assumption is incomplete.
Separating a Chinese factory is the easy part. The harder problem sits one or two tiers upstream, in the minerals and machines China controls. The realistic goal for this decade is not a China-free company but a China-insulated one.
SpaceX drew about a fifth of its 2025 revenue from the U.S. government. Tesla is the only wholly foreign-owned automaker in China, and its Chinese-built cars use more than 95% local parts from over 400 suppliers .
Combining a Pentagon contractor with a factory that depends on Beijing’s goodwill raises national-security alarms in both capitals; JPMorgan calls regulatory approval a “practical bottleneck.”
Tesla’s advisers have reportedly discussed a spin-off, sale or closure of the China business, though Musk dismissed the report as “absurdly fake news.”
Closure would sacrifice Tesla’s lowest-cost plant, a sale needs Beijing’s blessing and a spin-off may not look like a real break to Washington. The likeliest outcome is ring-fencing: separate entities, systems and staff. But these are corporate-structure problems, with corporate-structure solutions.
SpaceX has already shown what decoupling looks like. In August it began auditing suppliers worldwide , requiring them to keep Chinese-made equipment and Chinese nationals away from SpaceX work. It has lined up long-term nickel superalloy supply from Korea, sought non-Chinese polysilicon and pushed to build solar manufacturing in the United States. At the level of parts, factories and personnel, this works.
Look one or two tiers upstream, however, and China reappears.
SpaceX’s Korean alloy supplier sources nickel from an Indonesian project co-owned with an affiliate of China’s Tsingshan. China refines more than 90% of the world’s rare earths, and the International Energy Agency projects that refining capacity planned outside China will meet only about two-thirds of requirements by 2035.
China’s dominance of upstream supply chain operations is structural, not merely commercial.
In January, Musk pledged 100 gigawatts a year of U.S. solar-cell capacity. By March, Tesla was negotiating to buy $2.9 billion of Chinese equipment. In May, The New York Times reported that Beijing had blocked exports of high-end tools from Chinese company Suzhou Maxwell to Tesla. This month, China proposed banning exports of the technology and equipment for next-generation perovskite and tandem cells, while still selling the cells themselves.
The message is precise: China will sell Musk products, not the capacity to make them.
Rare earths carry a sharper deadline. In October 2025, Beijing announced rules requiring licenses for foreign-made products containing as little as 0.1% Chinese-origin rare earths by value. The rule was suspended for a year, and that suspension expires on November 10 . If it returns, a Japanese magnet bound for a Starlink satellite or an Optimus robot could need Beijing’s permission.
The leverage is asymmetric. Washington controls permission: contracts, clearances and market access. Beijing controls inputs, and with them cost and speed.
The bigger the combined company’s ambitions, the more that asymmetry bites.
A faster Starship cadence; a Starlink constellation approaching 10,000 active satellites; and plans for orbital data centers all demand magnets, gallium, solar wafers and specialty alloys in volumes that non-Chinese suppliers cannot yet deliver at comparable cost or speed.
Beijing also need not block the merger to shape it.
China can approve with conditions, such as safeguards on data from roughly two million Chinese Tesla drivers, while calibrating access to equipment and minerals. It can also simply wait: Intel abandoned its $5.4 billion purchase of Tower Semiconductor in 2023 after Chinese approval never arrived . And Tesla’s own bargaining power in China is eroding. Domestic retail sales fell 9% in September , and Leapmotor outsold Tesla China in June.
Decoupling buys security and eligibility for sensitive U.S. government work, but it carries a price premium and a long tail of indirect dependence. Investors should price that premium rather than assume China risk leaves with Shanghai. Allied suppliers in Korea, Japan and Europe will find themselves squeezed between American audits and Chinese licensing rules.
The special committees should treat upstream resilience as a deal term, not a footnote. That means mapping exposure to the third tier, building buffer inventories of magnets and gallium before November 10, and co-investing with allied refiners and equipment makers.
Washington should fund processing and toolmaking, not just assembly, because that is where China’s leverage lies.
A merged Tesla and SpaceX can control who builds its hardware. For the rest of this decade, China will still heavily influence what that hardware costs and how quickly it can scale.
Planning for insulation rather than independence is not defeatism. It is the only strategy the supply chain will allow in the foreseeable future.
Christopher Tang is a distinguished research professor at the UCLA Anderson School of Management .
A scholar of global supply chain management, Tang’s interest in his field began in the private sector when he worked for IBM to solve internal production planning problems. Exposure to real-life industry projects motivated his academic research, where he developed teaching cases on microfinancing for the poor, mobile platforms for developing economies and new business models in the age of the Internet, among other topics.
Tang has been a consultant to numerous corporations, including Amazon, HP, IBM, Nestlé  and Accenture. He has published six books and in addition to being a regular contributor to IndustryWeek , he has written for the Wall Street Journal , Barron’s, Financial Times , China Daily, Fortune, Bloomberg Law and The Guardian .

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Iran says indirect talks with U.S. on ceasefire proposal continue
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Iran says indirect talks with U.S. on ceasefire proposal continue
articles.content_orig:
The Saudi energy ministry said that falling debris from the interception of a drone targeting an oil facility killed two people and injured two others on Wednesday.
"The attempted attack resulted in the deaths of two individuals, a Filipino and a Nepali, and injuries to two others," the ministry said in a statement. It did not say who launched the drone aimed at the Shaybah oil field near the UAE border.
The U.S. has ordered all non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia as the kingdom faces escalating attacks by Houthi militants.
"Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a social media post Wednesday.
The order came a few days after the U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia , Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and several other countries warned that hostilities could rapidly and without warning spread beyond areas already affected by the fighting.
"The safety and security of Department personnel and their families remain our highest priority, and we will continue to take all necessary steps to protect and support them," Pigott added.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi issued a warning to the U.S. on Wednesday afternoon, saying it should choose diplomacy over returning to war.
"Iran is prepared to give diplomacy another chance if we see strong evidence of a sincere desire by US to build trust & reach a just solution," he wrote on X , sharing a link to an opinion piece in the Financial Times. "But if US chooses war over diplomacy, it'll certainly result in an even greater strategic failure."
Araghchi said earlier in the day that Iran and the U.S. were still involved in indirect negotiations via mediators over the seven-day ceasefire proposal from September. The proposal was outright rejected by President Trump, but Araghchi said the U.S. was trying to add further clauses to the agreement.
The U.S. Treasury announced new sanctions on the Panamanian-Greek law firm Karnakis and Karnakis for involvement in Iran's "shadow fleet" as part of its Operation Economic Outcast .
The U.S. accuses Karnakis and Karnakis of being indirectly involved in Iran's illicit shipping operations for years. A "shadow fleet" refers to oil tankers that hide their true ownership in order to evade sanctions.
"Whether you are conducting illegal oil transfers at sea or sitting in the corner office of a law firm, if you are supporting the Iranian regime, we will find you and sanction you," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. "Iran's facilitators must make a choice: Either you are with us or against us. We know who you are, we know what you're doing, and we will continue to take action."
The Treasury also said it sanctioned Singapore- and UAE-based shipping agents, including a fleet of cargo vessels that has directly taken part in Iran's "shadow fleet" and "helped generate substantial revenue for the Iranian regime."
A limited number of Saudi airlines took off and landed at the country's main airport on Wednesday, two days after authorities notified airlines that they could resume operations with prior permission.
Saudia and FlyNas were operating flights Wednesday, according to flight-tracking data published by FlightAware. Major carriers, including Lufthansa and Air France, have canceled flights through mid-November.
Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport has been hit multiple times this month by Yemen's Houthi rebels and shut down on Oct. 10. A strike two weeks ago killed 13 people and injured hundreds more.
The Houthis have acknowledged attacking the airport, claiming without evidence that Saudi Arabia provided military equipment to government forces through the facility.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said any interference in the Yemen war by Egypt or any other country would make the situation "more difficult."
"Egypt has sufficient experience to avoid entangling itself in such a highly complex conflict," said Iran's top diplomat in an interview with Iraqi state broadcaster Al-Iraqiya aired on Tuesday.
"We believe that any foreign presence or interference will only make resolving this issue more difficult," Araghchi noted.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Wednesday that Cairo's proposed military support for Riyadh was to "defend Saudi territory, and does not include an attack on Yemen," according to a statement from his office.
At a government event titled Egypt Forum 2026, Sisi said the "objective is to defend the kingdom's lands and borders, as well as those of any other Arab state, should it be requested of Egypt," his spokesman said in a statement.
Sisi on Saturday had asked parliament to authorize support for Saudi Arabia in its war with the Houthis, "if requested."
The parliament, which is stacked with supporters of the president, has since held two rare secret sessions, before postponing deliberations until next week.
Iran's newly appointed defense minister, Mehrdad Akhlaghi, said Wednesday his first hours in office were devoted to meeting the requirements of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' Aerospace Force and the army's air defense units.
"We are not in a war of rhetoric in response to repeated threats; we are turning threats into greater readiness and more effective defensive power," he wrote in his first post on X since taking office.
Akhlaghi added Iran was concentrating on its objectives through the use of new technologies.
"We may eat dirt, but we will not give up our soil," he concluded.
President Trump blocked a planned Israeli multiday operation that would have resumed strikes against Iran on the weekend of Oct. 10, according to the Financial Times .
The plan was designed to exceed the intensity of the joint U.S.-Israeli military offensive launched in February, three people familiar with the matter told the paper, and would have struck Iranian nuclear sites, regime targets and civilian infrastructure such as power plants.
The president blocked the strike to avoid escalating conflict before the U.S. midterm elections, according to the report.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Wednesday he had directed the Israeli army and intelligence services to topple the Iranian regime.
"The regime in Iran has still not learned the lesson," Netanyahu told a graduation ceremony at an officer training school in the country's southern Negev desert.
"Mojtaba Khamenei, the current tyrant, has decided to follow in his father's footsteps," he said, referring to the country's supreme leader, who replaced his father Ali Khamenei after he was killed in a U.S.-Israeli airstrike on Feb. 28.
"He has taken the safety off, and Iran is once again attempting to develop 'death bombs,'" he added, without giving details on what exactly he was referring to.
"There is only one way to remove this threat once and for all," Netanyahu said, "by toppling the regime in Iran. And that is my directive to the [Israel Defense Forces], the Mossad, and the security services."
He did not expand on how he expected the military or intelligence services to carry out the directive.
Saudi Arabia has held talks with a senior Syrian military delegation on arrangements to transfer up to 10,000 Syrian fighters to take part in the war against Yemen's Houthi movement, according to a report by the Lebanese Hezbollah-owned Al-Akhbar newspaper, citing Yemeni intelligence sources.
The report claims Syrian military officials visited Saudi Arabia's southern regions of Najran and Asir to inspect sites prepared to receive the fighters, while discussions in Riyadh covered transport logistics, financing and military assignments.
The Syrian delegation included Brig. Gen. Khaled Khattab, former commander of the Ansar al-Tawhid faction and current commander of the 82nd Division in the new Syrian army;

articles.title_orig: Meta earnings live updates: What analysts expect when the social media giant reports
articles.title_zh: Meta earnings live updates: What analysts expect when the social media giant reports
articles.content_orig:
A big rally in SpaceX after earnings is giving hope to Meta and Tesla bulls ahead of their reports due Wednesday afternoon.
Options trading in both stocks leaned bullish after the open Wednesday, with Meta options looking particularly one-sided as traders bought more calls than puts and more put trades likely initiated by sellers than buyers. More than 30,000 calls traded at or above the ask, suggesting they were bought, versus under 17,000 puts, Cboe LiveVol data shows.
Meta options have generally been bullish since the stock's March low, when the put/call ratio of open contracts plunged to 0.5, meaning two calls open for every one put contract, and that hasn't budged much since, Barchart data show. Almost $22 million of trades were done with a bullish intent on Wednesday, compared to $7.5 million looking for downside.
Market-makers are pricing a 6.5% swing for Meta after earnings, a little under the 9% average the past four quarters. The most popular contract to buy on Wednesday was the 800 strike call expiring Friday that costs $1.40 and needs Meta to rally 14% into the weekend, SpotGamma data shows.
In Tesla, the flows also lean bullish, but with less conviction. The put/call ratio of open contracts is 0.75, compared to Meta's 0.5, though more calls did trade Wednesday morning than puts.
Of the 520,000 contracts traded in Tesla, 315,000 were calls, as traders bought 88,000 calls and 65,000 puts, according to Cboe LiveVol data. There was also notable call-selling, with 83,000 call contracts likely sold and seven of the top 10 trades by dollar-amount call sales.
Still, traders spent more money buying calls than they did puts, with call-buying premiums amounting to over $200 million, compared to $84 million in puts, according to SpotGamma's analysis.
Market-makers are pricing a 5.5% swing in Tesla after its report, above the four-quarter median of 3.5%. That said, Tesla's last report caused a 14% selloff in the stock that makes the average move in that period 5.5%.
The most-heavily traded contracts by volume Wednesday were the 385 and 400-strike calls expiring Friday, with buyers favoring the cheaper 400-strike call and sellers leaning into the 385-strikes, SpotGamms data show.

Virginia Tech is accelerating the closure of a joint undergraduate programme with China’s Xidian University, bringing forward the end of a partnership that it had previously planned to keep running until 2029, according to a university spokesperson and a copy of an official letter reviewed by the South China Morning Post.
Margaret Ashburn, Virginia Tech’s associate director of media relations and deputy spokesperson, shared a copy of the school’s letter to the Pentagon and told SCMP that the university had recently decided to accelerate the closure of the joint programme with Xidian University.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Nasdaq Opens Higher; SpaceX Shares Surge on Tesla Deal Talks — Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Nasdaq Opens Higher; SpaceX Shares Surge on Tesla Deal Talks — Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX stock jumped 10% Wednesday after the company reported surging revenue growth in its third quarter, and owner Elon Musk floated a potential SpaceX- Tesla merger.
The space company, which made its debut on the Nasdaq in the biggest initial public offering ever in June, reported third-quarter revenue on Tuesday of $14.6 billion, up 161% from the previous year, and beating LSEG consensus estimates of $12.72 billion.
Meanwhile, its operating income came in at $2.8 billion, with net income of $4.4 billion, after reporting a net loss of $1.05 billion in the same period a year earlier.
On an earnings call, Musk said he's considering a combination with Tesla — which would mark the largest merger in history — and that the boards of both companies have created specific committees to discuss a consolidation.
"I do think there's a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there's a lot to be gained from cooperating," Musk said on the call. Tesla is set to report third-quarter earnings after the closing bell on Wednesday.
Shares of other space stocks, including Rocket Lab , Intuitive Machines and AST SpaceMobile climbed on Wednesday.
SpaceX forecasts first-quarter 2027 revenue between $33 billion and $37 billion, beating the average analyst estimate of $22.2 billion, according to LSEG.
"We delivered another strong quarter in Q3. Revenue grew an impressive 161% year-over-year, fueled by continued momentum in Connectivity and a clear inflection in our Super Intelligence business," SpaceX's chief financial officer, Bret Johnsen, said in the earnings release.
Johnsen pinned the strong results on recurring revenue from its satellite internet business, Starlink , and significant expansion of its Super Intelligence [SI] infrastructure.
The company has dived into artificial intelligence this year, which it's now calling SI. The segment is its largest business unit, with revenue soaring ninefold to $7.56 billion from $813 million in the same quarter last year.
Commentary on computing during the earnings call supported "continued pricing power and shorter payback periods" for AI cloud providers, Truist Securities analysts said in a Tuesday note.
"Despite market concerns relating to financing for AI cloud providers this past week, we believe SpaceX's third-quarter 2026 represents the first data point during the earnings season to support the bull case for AI cloud providers," they added.
They explained that demand appears "insatiable," with SpaceX noting that it could rent out its capacity several times over. The analysts said Coreweave and Nebius are set to benefit and capture demand as "pricing power will more than offset higher rates."
The shares of neoclouds Nebius and Coreweave traded marginally lower, while Iren and Applied Digital climbed in early trading on Wednesday.
— CNBC's Lora Kolodny contributed to this report.
Correction: Bret Johnsen is chief financial officer at SpaceX. An earlier version misspelled his name.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo needs no further lung cancer treatment, Vatican says
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo needs no further lung cancer treatment, Vatican says
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV's brother Louis Prevost shares updates on the pope's recovery following cancer removal surgery. He discusses the pope's first public prayer and messages of support from Rome.
Pope Leo XIV will need no further treatment for lung cancer after final tests confirmed the disease was localized, his doctors said Wednesday.
Dr. Luigi Carbone and Professor Stefano Margaritora announced the findings just over a week after surgeons removed a tumor from the pontiff’s right lung.
"The final histopathology and molecular testing reports on the tissue removed during the Holy Father’s surgery were issued today," the doctors said in a statement.
POPE LEO WELCOMED BACK AS HE DELIVERS ANGELUS PRAYER DAYS AFTER LUNG CANCER SURGERY
"The results confirmed that the tumor was a lung adenocarcinoma and that the disease was localized. A subsequent oncological assessment has confirmed that no further treatment is necessary."
Pope Leo underwent surgery Oct. 13 at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital. The operation lasted about 90 minutes, with the pope spending approximately three hours in the operating room, according to the Holy See.
"The doctors said it was successful and there were no complications," the Holy See press office said after the procedure.
The pontiff awoke normally and returned to his hospital room following a brief observation period, Vatican News reported.
RECOVERING FROM LUNG SURGERY, POPE LEO URGES PUTIN TO AGREE TO CEASEFIRE IN RUSSIAN-HELD UKRAINE CITY
Pope Leo XIV addresses the crowd during the weekly general audience at St Peter's Square in Vatican City, on October 21, 2026. (Massimo Valicchia/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
He was discharged Saturday after blood tests and a chest X-ray confirmed he was well enough to return to the Vatican. Thousands of supporters gathered outside the hospital, shouting "Papa!" as he departed.
Before leaving, Leo visited the children’s oncology ward, where young patients had sent him letters during his hospital stay.
POPE LEO'S LUNG TUMOR RAISES QUESTIONS ABOUT CANCER RISK FOR NONSMOKERS
Pope Leo reacts while sitting in a car as he leaves Gemelli Hospital following his lung surgery and cancer diagnosis, in Rome, Italy, October 17, 2026. (Remo Casilli/Reuters)
"Pope Leo, our prayers are for you," a girl named Eleonora wrote in a letter released by Vatican News.
"May God, the Most Holy Virgin, and the guardian angels always protect you," she added.
Eleonora’s mother told the pope her daughter was now healthy, according to the Vatican.

"Faith moves mountains," Eleonora wrote. "God has heard our prayers."
Fox News Digital's Robert McGreevy contributed to this report.

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.
Los Angeles County election officials say that the Justice Department's list of 20,000 "likely" noncitizens registered to vote is "unreliable," based on their preliminary analysis . They also say some of the individuals on the list have indicated they were born in the U.S. and may be citizens. State and local officials disclosed these new details in court filings yesterday, in response to a federal lawsuit demanding that California investigate thousands of voters before their ballots are counted. The DOJ wants the state to segregate ballots associated with these individuals. California officials say the DOJ's request is unfeasible so close to the election and may violate federal and state election laws.
People vote at a polling location at the Metro Headquarters Building during California's state primary election in Los Angeles, California, on June 2, 2026. Frederic J. Brown/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
A new report from United Nations scientists says that countries are not doing enough to cut emissions that drive climate change, and the United States plays a significant role in climate pollution. The U.S. was the only major economy that saw an increase last year in planet-warming pollution. The report also found that, among G20 countries, the U.S. is tied with Russia for the highest per capita emissions. While China emits more total greenhouse gases annually than the U.S., China's population is more than four times that of the U.S. The rise in U.S. emissions was fueled by increased electricity demand and Trump administration policies that support burning fossil fuels.
Arrests for low-level crimes, including vagrancy and drug possession, increased in the U.S. from 2024 to 2025, according to a new analysis of federal data from the criminal justice and immigration reforms advocacy group FWD.us. The report also highlighted a 188% increase in immigration violations. This comes as violent crime rates, including homicides, dropped to historic lows. The report examined publicly available FBI and immigration arrest data and does not include details about whether charges were dropped or if people served any time in jail or prison. This data covers the first full year of Trump's second term, during which his administration emphasized a tough-on-crime approach. Zoë Towns, the executive director of FWD.us, told NPR ahead of the report's release that the rising trends signal a "really troubling return to some of the extreme law and order policies that defined the American criminal justice system during the '80s and '90s." Check out NPR's analysis .
President Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff is in St. Petersburg today to meet with Kremlin officials and explore potential solutions for ending Russia's war on Ukraine. Witkoff also met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy this week in Norway. Trump has accused Zelenskyy of obstructing a peace deal. The Ukrainian president says he is again seeking direct talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The results of the 2026 midterm elections will shape the final two years of President Trump's second term and serve as a precursor to the 2028 general election. This month, Morning Edition is reporting from six states that could change the balance of power in Washington.
This week, Morning Edition 's Steve Inskeep traveled to North Carolina and Georgia. Both states are among those Trump visited this week as he continues to campaign for Republicans vying to keep control of the Senate and House. Inskeep explored how the Trump administration's policies have affected public research in both states. Trump has eliminated hundreds of jobs from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, which is headquartered in Atlanta. Universities and research firms in North Carolina's Research Triangle lost millions of dollars in federal grants last year. Inskeep spoke with people affected by these changes. Listen to what they had to say .

Follow the reporting: Ohio and Michigan coverage airs Oct. 27. You can follow along on Morning Edition , NPR.org, in the NPR app and in this newsletter.
by Tommy Evans , NPR's editor in chief
To cover a transformation as vast as AI, one that raises deep questions about work, culture, the environment, cybersecurity, education and so much more, we've teamed up with veteran tech journalists Casey Newton and Kevin Roose to bring their flagship AI podcast, Machine Gods , to NPR's audiences. Starting today, the video-first program will be offered twice a week across NPR's platforms and provide front-row access to the people and issues shaping this new AI era.
The show will look into things like the ways AI could be applied to the medical field, potentially helping us discover new drugs and improve healthcare overall, as well as the questions that keep Casey and Kevin both up at night, like what happens when AI eventually builds and improves upon itself beyond what humans understand. With each episode, we'll make sure you get the news you need to know about AI — both the technology's capabilities and its very real risks — without buying into the industry's hype or treating catastrophe as an inevitability.
Machine Gods is the culmination of years of Casey and Kevin's reporting from the front lines of Silicon Valley. While it represents an ambitious new format for public media, its core ethos fits seamlessly with NPR's mission: to bring audiences trusted, independent journalism that inspires, engages, and keeps you informed so you can navigate the world with confidence.
You can see the first episode here .

articles.title_orig: Meta Ordered to Pay $25 Billion for Deceiving Users on Privacy
articles.title_zh: Meta Ordered to Pay $25 Billion for Deceiving Users on Privacy
articles.content_orig:
Meta was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties by a New Mexico court on Wednesday as part of a data privacy case that stemmed from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago.
The penalty, revealed in a court filing, comes after a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse found in September the social media giant liable for misleading state citizens about how it safeguards and collects user data and prevents harmful information from flourishing on its services.
Although the jury concluded that Meta had more than 43 million violations of the state's unfair practices act, with each transgression carrying a civil penalty as high as $5,000, a New Mexico judge was responsible for determining the ultimate fine. The Wednesday filing showed that the state was awarded $219.5 billion, but the penalty was ultimately reduced to $25 billion.
"The extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership, the size of New Mexico audiences reached, and the clear intentional and systematic nature of Facebook's repeated misstatements established in the trial record support the highest level of penalty allowed by the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act - $5,000 per violation found by the jury," New Mexico District Court Judge Francis Mathew wrote in the filing.
The judge added that interest on the penalty shall accrue at the rate of 15% each year until the fine is paid off in full.
"For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," said New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez in a statement.
He added that "this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences."
Meta chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney criticized the penalty, saying in a statement that the company is "confident" that it will "prevail on appeal."
"This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said in the statement. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online."
Meta previously resolved various Cambridge Analytica-derived data privacy lawsuits across the nation as part of an overarching August settlement of nearly $17 billion with a coalition of state attorneys general in a separate federal case related to child safety and mental health. But because New Mexico was not part of the settlement, the state's data privacy case that arose from Meta's Cambridge Analytica scandal proceeded to trial in September.
In 2022, the social media giant agreed to pay $725 million to settle a class action lawsuit that also sprang from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal that kicked off in 2018. That scandal rocked the Mark Zuckerberg -led company before its official name change to Meta, and focused on allegations that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica improperly accessed the information of 87 million users , raising questions about Facebook's data handling practices.
Mathew said in the filing that "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations.
"Pressure from senior executives to keep costs down, lack of adequate enforcement resources, inadequate investigative techniques, and a desire not to create precedent for future investigations," all contributed to what the judge characterized as a "willfully ineffective" internal examination by Facebook, the filing said.
Former New Mexico Attorney General Hector Balderas originally filed the state's Cambridge Analytica-related lawsuit in 2021, while current AG Torrez oversaw the related trial.
Torrez also led his state's child safety-related trial against Meta that resulted in a March jury ruling that the social media company should pay $375 million for violating the state's unfair practices act. A New Mexico judge would later order Meta to pay $567 million into an abatement fund as part of a second phase of the case that determined the social media firm's actions created a public nuisance.
Meta said it disagreed with that New Mexico ruling and planned to appeal.

articles.title_orig: Xbox mandates a four-day return to office
articles.title_zh: Xbox mandates a four-day return to office
articles.content_orig:
Xbox employees close to Microsoft’s Redmond headquarters will need to come into the office more starting in February.
Xbox employees close to Microsoft’s Redmond headquarters will need to come into the office more starting in February.
Microsoft asked its employees to return to the office three days per week last year , and it’s now upping this requirement to four days a week for most Xbox employees. An internal memo, seen by The Verge , describes the change as a “need to create more opportunities for people to work together” after feedback from Xbox employees.
“Starting February 1st, 2027, Xbox employees in Puget Sound who live within 50 commuting miles of Studio D are required to work from the office a minimum of four days a week,” says Jacinda Chislum Pearson, Xbox chief people officer, in the internal memo. “We have thousands of Xbox employees within commuting distance of Redmond. Taking advantage of that proximity and working together in person makes it easier to review work, resolve issues, and make decisions without the burden of scheduling another meeting.”
The change to four days in the office will only apply to those close to Microsoft’s corporate campus in Redmond, Washington, and Pearson’s memo appears to suggest that “established in-office practices” for Xbox studios will remain unchanged.
Microsoft has had exemptions to its return to office rules for certain roles, and Xbox employees with existing exemptions will need to resubmit them again. The return to office changes come just a day after a report suggested Microsoft was planning to announce further Xbox layoffs this month , and in November and January. Microsoft announced in July that it was planning to eliminate around 20 percent of Xbox jobs by the end of its financial year at the end of June 2027.
Xbox is also positioning its updated return to office policy as one that “should be worth the investment” of taking the time to commute into the office, especially for those 40-50 miles away. “Leaders should be present, and coming into the office should not mean spending the same day on Teams calls from a different building,” says Pearson. “Time well spent means reviewing work, solving problems, and playing games together, strengthening our path to becoming one Xbox.”

Dozens of Israel Air Force fighter jets flew "as far as the Iranian border" before turning around and returning to Israel in a practice sortie on Monday, according to an Axios report on Wednesday citing US and Israeli officials.
The fighter jets and accompanying refueling aircraft allegedly passed through Syrian and Iraqi airspace, following a flight path consistent with that taken during strikes on Iran.
While some sources told Axios that the sortie was not unusual and was intended to deter Iran, US officials said that Israel knew Iran’s air defense systems would detect the jets.
Israel reportedly notified the US of the operation in advance, describing the training exercise as a “power projection” aimed at deterring Iran from attacking Israel ahead of the October 27 Knesset elections.
On Tuesday, Fox News’ Trey Yingst also reported that Israeli fighter jets had conducted drills during which they flew over Syria and Iraq.

articles.title_orig: New clues in Westminster Abbey mystery: Medieval skeleton buried in Roman-era sarcophagus finally identified
articles.title_zh: New clues in Westminster Abbey mystery: Medieval skeleton buried in Roman-era sarcophagus finally identified
articles.content_orig:
They’re lifting the lid on this centuries-old mystery.
The identity of a mysterious skeleton discovered at Westminster Abbey in London has potentially been revealed — more than 150 years since its discovery.
“We have two viable contenders,” Professor Warwick Rodwell, the Consultant Archaeologist at Westminster Abbey who led the study, Livescience reported.
These remains were reportedly found in a stone sarcophagus that had been unearthed by the landmark’s chief mason in 1820, per a study published in the Journal Of The British Archaeological Association . Workers had inadvertently stumbled upon it while digging on the north side of the abbey for an undisclosed project — and accidentally smashed the lid into six pieces.
Unfortunately, expert analysis revealed that the vessel was looted earlier in that century, leading researchers to initially believe it was bereft of bones .
The incident wasn’t officially recorded until 1869, when they finally repaired the stone.
That’s when they noticed a Roman-style carving on the side of the vessel with a Latin inscription dedicated “to the memory of Valerius Amandinus.”
This would appear to indicate that the occupant was Roman, except there was a massive cross carved into the sarcophagus’ lid, suggesting that the tomb was repurposed for a dignified religious figure’s interment centuries later.
This mystery eluded archaeologists for 150 years until 2016, when the vessel was opened for conservation, revealing that it indeed housed a skeleton.
While the bones had been tampered with over the years — with a hole in the skull and jumbled arm and leg bones — it was apparent that they belonged to a middle-aged male of average height, who also had a history of gout , rib injuries and osteoarthritis.
Using carbon dating, the researchers were able to deduce that he lived between 987 and 1052, confirming that the Roman-era sarcophagus had been repurposed.
But who was the occupant? To get to the bottom, Rodwell examined the birth and death dates of the Westminster abbots along with their tenure, eventually whittling the pool down to two candidates.
They were Ælfwig, who served from 993 to 1020, and his successor Wulfnoth, who held the position from 1020 to 1049.
“We do not know the date of birth of either,” said Rodwell, per the Daily Mail. “But either would fit equally well if we assume the Abbot was in his early 20s when the appointment was made and close to 50 when he died.”
He added, “The fact Aelfwig was already a monk of Westminster might favor him.”
However, the nature of the burial remains perplexing.
Rodwell noted that the recycling of Roman sarcophagi is highly unorthodox — with no comparable cases ever documented — although he feels a clue may lie in the inscription itself.
The scientists noted that the “memoriae” (to the memory) on the box might indicate Valerius Amandinus was an early Christian himself who may have been a big player in Roman London.
“Unfortunately, nothing is known about his career,” Rodwell lamented.

The talks in a grand imperial palace in St Petersburg, the ninth time that Witkoff has met Putin in person, began with a goodwill gesture from Russia – the release of Stephen Hubbard, a retired US teacher held in Russia.
President Donald Trump confirmed the release in a social media post, saying the United States was not required to give anything in return.
Hubbard was first detained in April 2022 and was later sentenced to six years and 10 months on charges whose veracity his family and US-based lawyer question.

articles.title_orig: Just Eat apologises for AI food mistakes after social media ridicule
articles.title_zh: Just Eat apologises for AI food mistakes after social media ridicule
articles.content_orig:
Just Eat has apologised after it was ridiculed online over a series of mistakes with AI-generated pictures for some of its restaurants' food items.
The online food delivery platform had been testing out the tech to showcase food which didn't have images yet - but not all turned out as planned.
Instead the AI invented several bizarre concoctions, from bacon and eggs floating in a glass of cola - a confusion between "soda" and "soda bread" - to chips poking out of muffins.
A Just Eat spokesperson said the firm was "in the process of removing" the incorrect images, and would stop making more until the AI was further developed.
"We work with tens of thousands of small restaurants on their food imagery, including funding professional local photographers," the spokesperson told the BBC.
"We've been trialling AI-enhanced images, and as with any new technology, it isn't always quite right the first time."
The incident highlights the difficulties companies can still face when using AI to speed up or simplify work processes, especially when it is used to interpret words in a specific context.
Members of the Just Eat UK subreddit have flocked to the site over the past few days to post the latest unintentionally hilarious spins on takeaway food items.
Any picture generated using AI on the delivery app appears with a label indicating so, and the BBC has spotted many of the more unusual takes still up on menus.
A Belfast cafe, meanwhile, had its bacon and egg soda bread dish represented as a glass of fizzy drink with a cooked egg and bacon floating in it.
Spelling mistakes on menu items have sometimes added to the confusion, with the Instagram account @uknewestfoods posting a picture of garlic bread in the shape of a plane - presumably because of a misspelling of the word "plain".
Meanwhile, a "cheese roll" - bread and cheese - instead became slabs of cheese rolled into a sushi roll.
While some on social media said they found the images "hilarious", another was less interested in the AI-generated dishes, saying: "Well, that lot just helped my diet".
Meanwhile, one person on Instagram questioned why customers would ever want to see AI images of a restaurant's food even if they were closer to the real thing.
"I want to see what the dish actually looks like as it helps me decide who to order from or what to order," they said.
"These 'perfect' AI versions just lead to disappointment if that's what you think your meal will look like."

The Energy Department plans to loan 315,000 barrels from the 1 million barrel Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve, according to a statement Wednesday. Deliveries are scheduled to be completed by Nov. 13.
"This is a temporary measure to solve a temporary supply disruption," Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in the statement.
The average price of diesel, which has hit record highs during the Iran war, is about $6.32 a gallon, according to AAA. About 4% of the nation's households use heating oil, including in Maine, New Hampshire and Alaska — all of which are politically competitive.
The diesel fuel reserve, housed in commercial storage facilities across the Northeast, was used in the aftermath of Hurricane Sandy in 2012 to provide fuel for emergency responders in New York and New Jersey, as well as in the wake of snowstorms that same year.
Created under former President Bill Clinton, the reserve is designed to provide the Northeast 10 days of supply, which is roughly the time it takes for ships to bring additional heating oil from the Gulf of Mexico to New York Harbor, according to the Energy Department.
The Trump administration last year proposed selling the reserve, which the Energy Department estimated would generate $100 million.
Wright said in the statement that the governors of New York and New England should approve a proposed pipeline that the Trump administration is pushing to build to bring more natural gas to the region.

articles.title_orig: Buffett’s Berkshire just trounced chip stocks and flashed a rare dot-com-era signal
articles.title_zh: Buffett’s Berkshire just trounced chip stocks and flashed a rare dot-com-era signal
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
For three weeks, Wall Street sold the hottest trade in the market and bought one of the oldest. Chip stocks lost 15% while Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway gained 7%.
That swing carried Berkshire's Class B stock ( BRK-B ) to a record close Tuesday, its first since May 2, 2025 — the day before Buffett said he would hand the CEO job to Greg Abel. The stock pushed to an intraday record Wednesday, as did the Class A stock ( BRK-A ).
The wait took 17 months, a stretch in which the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) gained more than 35%.
From Oct. 6 through Tuesday, the iShares Semiconductor ETF ( SOXX ) fell in 10 of 11 sessions. Berkshire rose on nine of those days, and on chips' two worst days, Oct. 14 and Oct. 16, it posted two of its best gains of the run.
For now, that price action has made Berkshire look like a hedge against the AI chip trade. Since Oct. 1, it has mostly risen on the days chips fell.
Berkshire is on track to rise in 14 of its last 15 sessions. Along the way, it strung together a 10-day winning streak, its first since 2018, according to Yahoo Finance calculations.
From Oct. 2 through Tuesday, Berkshire beat SOXX by 22 percentage points. That's the widest gap over any 12-session stretch since early 2010, according to Yahoo Finance calculations that compare Berkshire with the PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) back to 1994. The 12-session window is the one that captures this month's widest gap.
The rarer signal is the combination.
Chips fell at least 14% while Berkshire gained at least 7% over 12 sessions. Before this month, that last happened Oct. 3, 2001. Every earlier case came in 1995-96 or in 2000-01, the latter as the dot-com bubble burst.
History sends a mixed message from here.
In the near term, chips bounced. They were higher a week later in five of the six earlier cases, and they're rebounding Wednesday,too. A year out, chips were lower in five of six instances, and the S&P 500 fell in four.
Four of those six cases came during the same bear market, though. Treat this as a rare signal, not a forecast.
Abel has also changed how Berkshire uses its cash. Berkshire bought back about $4.5 billion of its own stock in the second quarter and ended 14 straight quarters of net stock selling while its cash pile fell from a record $397 billion.
Buffett said Sept. 18 he would also step down as chairman. The stock bottomed two weeks later.
The next test comes with third quarter results, expected to be released Saturday, Nov. 7.

articles.title_orig: Australian politician who was hit by car has lost both legs
articles.title_zh: Australian politician who was hit by car has lost both legs
articles.content_orig:
Helen Haines, the Australian MP who was hit by a car in what authorities say was a deliberate attack, has lost both her legs, her husband has confirmed.
Phil Haines said the "horrendous incident" caused his wife significant injuries but "her heart and her mind are in good shape". He added that the "good news in all this is that she's alive".
The alleged attacker, 43-year-old Brendan Nugent, faces multiple charges and appeared in court for the first time on Wednesday.
Nugent was arrested moments after he allegedly drove his Toyota LandCruiser into the independent MP outside her electorate office in the regional town of Wangaratta, about 240km (150miles) northeast of Melbourne.
Haines' "road to recovery will be long and difficult, but we know she is a fighter," her husband said at a press conference in Melbourne where she is being treated.
"She is a determined person who will do her best, with our support and love, to recover. And that is what we hope for."
He thanked hospital staff and people, both in Australia and internationally, who have shown their concern for Haines, and urged those who want to show their support to donate to the Save the Children fund.
"Please keep sending Helen your love," he added.
Earlier on Wednesday, Nugent appeared at the local court to face three charges: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official. Police said more charges may be laid, including attempted murder.
Nugent - a local from the nearby town of Tarrawingee and known as an environmental campaigner - remained silent and emotionless during his brief court appearance.
He did not apply for bail and is due back in court in February. Court documents show he was also charged with cultivating and possessing cannabis.
In court, Nugent's lawyer said that his client had "mental health concerns" but did not give any further detail.
The court also heard that Nugent has a rare neurological condition - idiopathic transverse myelitis - caused by inflammation of the spinal cord.
Victoria Police said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police (AFP), remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established.
"His motivation for this - what we allege is a deliberate attack - is very much a centrepiece of the investigation," said Victoria Police Commissioner Mike Bush.
"Our people will continue to explore every element, angle and avenue to work that out. It's something that, when we work towards it, discover it, we will present in court."
Nugent was not on the radar of police and there was no intelligence of any threat to Haines before the incident, police said.
Investigators are also looking into whether drug use or medication played a part in the incident and if there was any personal connection between Nugent and Haines.
Nugent's family earlier put out a statement saying they were long-time friends with Haines, who is the independent MP for the regional seat of Indi in Victoria. They described the apparent attack as "devastating and unfathomable".
The incident occurred on Monday afternoon at around 15.35, local time. Moments after the car hit Haines, bystanders pulled Nugent out of the vehicle and detained him.
Jacob and Jackie Evans were among the first on the scene, and said Haines was grateful to them for coming to her aid as she lay severely injured.
"Thank you, you lovely people," is what Haines said to them, according to the Herald Sun.
"She was thanking us, it was incredible," Jackie told Nine's Today programme.
Jacob used a tourniquet he had in a medical kit in his car to help stem the bleeding from one of Haines's legs.
Haines underwent surgery after the incident and lost one of her legs. As of Wednesday morning she has also lost the other leg, her husband Phil told reporters.
The community in Wangaratta, as well as the wider political community, are in shock over the incident in a country where political violence is rare.
Leaders from across the political spectrum have paid tribute to Haines, who was first elected in 2019 and is well regarded by her peers.
Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he had spoken to Haines's husband several times since the incident.
In an interview with the national broadcaster ABC, Albanese said threats to female politicians were marked by a "different form of vilification and aggression" such as threats of rape.
There has also been a recent growing trend of threats against "high office holders", with almost one person a week being charged for such offences, police said.
Monday's incident has sparked debate over the level of security for MPs.
Federal police said that individual protection for every one of the country's 226 federal MPs would require "incredible" levels of staffing.
Instead, police assess the need for close personal protection based on a person's role and the threat environment around them, police said.
Australia's Governor-General Sam Mostyn, who spoke at the same press conference as Haines' husband, said this was "a moment for us to pause, and to choose to be better".
"We should do what I imagine Helen would be doing if she was not the victim of this terrible attack - reaching out to those who are terribly distressed by what has happened," she says.
"Most importantly, that we learn or re-learn to exercise our muscle of decency."

articles.title_orig: What We Saw at Fast-Track Trials of Riot Suspects in France
articles.title_zh: What We Saw at Fast-Track Trials of Riot Suspects in France
articles.content_orig:
France is on fire, and it faces a political and an economic reckoning that feels dangerously familiar to Americans.
The country is nearing a fiscal crisis, because it spent more than it can afford to pay back. The bill is coming due much faster than expected after bond rates surged in recent months, boosted by rising energy costs. Raising taxes and reducing government spending are part of a potential solution, but those would be politically unpopular decisions that could risk further angering an already livid public . Any workable solution faces a steep climb in an uncertain budget battle in a sharply divided government.
A growing number of countries are facing struggles similar to France’s — in particular, the United Kingdom — where rapidly growing debt, surging costs to finance that borrowing and insufficient political will to make the uncomfortable decisions to solve the problem are the story of Western economics right now. That includes the United States.
But similarities can be superficial.
France’s financial stress is particularly acute. The risk of contagion throughout Europe is low. France’s enormous public safety net represents a much larger share of government spending than that in the United States. And the unique dynamics of the American economy means the United States faces no imminent danger of becoming the next France.
These are not new problems: Europe’s social safety net has been on an unsustainable path for decades, and economists and some politicians have warned for years that the bill would eventually come due.
But they’re getting worse. The Iran war exacerbated the West’s fiscal problems.
Since February, the G7 economies’ average 10-year government bond yield grew more than 1 percentage point, reaching the highest level in nearly 20 years, the International Monetary Fund reported last week.
By the end of the decade, those seven economies’ public debt loads are expected to collectively exceed their economic production, the IMF predicts. That would be the first time since World War II.
France’s public debt is around 119% of its GDP, double the European Union’s target, and its annual budget deficit is 5.4% of its gross domestic product.
“In Europe, people are increasingly scared of the bond market and the interest rates that governments need to pay to borrow,” said Peter Taylor-Gooby, a social policy professor at the University of Kent. “It’s come to a point where you can’t ignore it anymore. If we do, we’ll reach a serious crisis.”
The rioting across France is a symptom of a much larger public and political crisis
On paper, America doesn’t look dissimilar: Its $32 trillion public debt is roughly equal to annual US GDP, and the $2 trillion budget deficit that it just closed the books on is more than 6% of GDP. The cost to finance America’s public debt just crossed $1 trillion a year , an astounding 14% of the total federal budget.
In other words, one in every seven tax dollars is used just to pay interest on the amount of money the United States is borrowing.
But the serious conversations about cutting back on spending and raising taxes taking place in Europe are considerably less serious in the United States. So why isn’t the United States facing the same problems as France?
The United States’ biggest advantage is that it prints the world’s reserve currency. The majority of global transactions are conducted in US dollars, including key commodities like oil and gold.
Demand for dollars remains robust in large part because they’re considered safe: The United States’ transparency and commitment to the rule of law make the dollar the cornerstone of the global financial system — even if some of the shine has worn off over the past decade.
That also fuels demand for US Treasuries, widely considered the safest of safe-haven assets. Even in the midst of a global government bond sell-off, US bond rates remain lower than those of other Western economies. And when stocks went on a skid last week, investors were unafraid to turn to their traditional place of refuge, sending Treasury yields sharply lower in the process.
But the difference between France and the United States really comes down to one thing. As James Carville said: It’s the economy, stupid.
The United States also has a uniquely large and diverse economy that is far less susceptible to shocks than many of its smaller peers. AI in particular is producing an investment boom in the United States that is lifting the economy when several other sectors appear to be stagnating or in decline.
One key way to make deficits less relevant is to keep the economy growing strong. That makes the debt look puny by comparison.
So countries need to ask: What is the rate we’re paying — and is it sustainable for us to keep paying it based on our expected economic growth?”
“France and the UK are pretty close,” noted Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s Analytics. “But in the US, AI’s contributions to growth make it more likely we’ll manage our debts and navigate it much more gracefully.”
Economists warn: Don’t confuse the lack of a looming debt crisis in the United States with fiscal responsibility. It’s just that it can handle the problem better than France or the UK.
“That doesn’t mean we should take any solace in that,” added Zandi. “We’re just in a different place.”
Any time a European country faces a fiscal problem, it raises concerns about a contagion that could spread across the continent. But economists widely view France’s problems as contained within the country.
The European Central Bank has signaled it would not need to intervene in France’s fiscal situation. But it could if it had to, and it is well-positioned to buy up a bunch of bonds of its member countries to limit any potential contagion effects, noted Andrew Kenningham, chief Europe economist at Capital Economics.
Other European economies’ deficits are also much smaller by comparison. Some are expected to run surpluses this year.
And French political parties across the left and right have said they want to remain with the European Union — including French presidential frontrunner Marine Le Pen, a far-right candidate who once championed “Frexit” but has since backed off that pledge. Although Germany’s AfD party has advocated leaving the EU, it isn’t close to forming a government yet, Kenningham noted.
But an X factor could lead to a debt crisis outside France: the US “X date.” At some point next year, the United States will hit its debt ceiling again, and the new Congress will need to negotiate with President Donald Trump to raise it — a political football that could be particularly challenged by a lame duck president and a potentially Democratic-controlled Congress less willing to give in.
A failure to raise the debt ceiling threatens to force the United States to manufacture a default on its debt, even if it otherwise would be able to pay.
“You could construct a scenario in which we breach the debt limit by Halloween next year,” said Zandi. “And then you’ve got other issues.”

articles.title_orig: SpaceX to attempt Starship catch on next flight, with eye on rapid cadence increase
articles.title_zh: SpaceX to attempt Starship catch on next flight, with eye on rapid cadence increase
articles.content_orig:
In its current iteration, SpaceX is largely a data company seeking to provide enormous amounts of compute for artificial intelligence. During an earnings call on Tuesday afternoon, company officials spent much of their time discussing ambitious plans to roll out up to 10 GW of compute in 2027—on the ground.
Gone are the days of aspirational talk about sending humans to Mars and settling the red planet. Now it is almost all about artificial intelligence and the data needed to support its expansion. However, the company’s long-term ambitions to provide data services from space, initially with the Starlink Internet constellation and eventually through the “Starmind” data center constellation, still rely on an actual rocket.
That would be the Starship vehicle, and during the earnings call, SpaceX founder Elon Musk and the company’s president and chief operating officer, Gwynne Shotwell, provided new performance targets for the vehicle.
It has been a little more than three weeks since the 14th test flight of the massive rocket, which largely went well despite some issues with the Raptor rocket engine. SpaceX has gleaned enough data from that test, Musk said, to attempt a catch of both the Super Heavy first stage of the rocket and the Starship upper stage on the next flight.
Musk said he believes success is “more likely than not” for these attempts, but he added the company is hardware rich if there are failures. Both catches would happen at the company’s launch site in South Texas, Starbase. SpaceX is currently targeting November for this 15th test flight.
One of the big hurdles is regulatory, as the Starship vehicle must return to the launch site over land, including northern Mexico.
“We have had significant constructive engagement with the FAA, and we expect the license for our Flight 15 to include return to launch site and tower catch for both stages,” Shotwell said.
As for what comes after this test flight, Shotwell said SpaceX would attempt to refly a Starship upper stage “early” next year. The company will also seek to complete a long-delayed refueling test of Starship early in 2027. This Starship-to-Starship refueling demonstration is an important milestone for SpaceX and NASA to prove the viability of Starship being refueled in low-Earth orbit for lunar missions.
Refueling on this scale has never been done before, and the company needs to get data on the efficiency of such transfers and the rate of boil-off of liquid oxygen and methane in space. This data will refine projections for how many launches are needed to support a Starship landing on the Moon for NASA as part of the Artemis Program.
For SpaceX, the near-term priority is reaching a high flight cadence for Starship and pushing the boundaries of vehicle reuse to enable it.
Musk, who often offers hyper-optimistic timeframes, said he expects Starship to reach a “weekly” flight cadence during the first half of 2027 and to launch twice weekly during the second half of the year. The key will be how much Starship can be reused.
“The rate at which we launch Starship will increase dramatically as we solve rapid and complete reusability,” Musk said. “At first there will be a little bit of refurbishment that’s needed between each flight, and we’ll iron out the need for any refurbishment such that you can immediately land the rocket and launch it again, just like an airplane.”
That’s the vision, at least. Achieving complete reusability with an orbital rocket has never been done before, so SpaceX’s engineering team will undoubtedly face some significant hurdles. Over time, however, they are likely to get close to the vision of launching, landing, and reflying rockets.
SpaceX will largely focus on its own payloads in 2027 with the Starship rocket. Shotwell said the company would continue launching Starlink V3 satellites, the second generation of “mobile” satellites that deliver direct-to-cell connectivity, as well as Starmind data center prototypes, next year. During the earnings call, neither Musk nor Shotwell addressed, nor were asked by financial analysts, about the controversial throttling of Starlink capabilities for Ukraine in its war with Russia.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | Senators Express ‘Grave Concerns,’ Launch Inquiry into Google’s AI Push in Schools
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | Senators Express ‘Grave Concerns,’ Launch Inquiry into Google’s AI Push in Schools
articles.content_orig:
The letter asks Google CEO Sundar Pichai to respond by Nov. 2 on what the company knows about AI's effect on students
Kevin Carter / Getty Images
Sens. Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat, and Josh Hawley, a Missouri Republican, sent a letter to Google $GOOGL CEO Sundar Pichai asking what the company knows about how its AI products affect the mental health of kids and their growth as learners, according to The Wall Street Journal .
The senators wrote that they have "grave concern" that Google 's "aggressive push of A.I. products to children in schools is threatening the academic success and overall wellbeing of an entire generation." They set a Nov. 2 deadline for Google to reply.
The letter asks Pichai how much Google understands about the ways its AI tools might harm children, why AI features were made the default setting on school devices, which worries districts, teachers and parents have voiced about students leaning on AI academically and emotionally, and which promotions Google has used to broaden the use of AI in schools.
" Google is forcing their A.I. products into classrooms across America, and children are paying the price," the senators wrote, according to The Wall Street Journal. "We cannot repeat the mistakes of social media platforms where products are pushed onto children putting profit ahead of young peoples' best interest."
The letter cites a September Wall Street Journal investigation. Drawing on more than 60 conversations with educators, school officials, parents, students and clinicians, the investigation found that many students have grown emotionally and academically reliant on Google 's AI tools, according to The Wall Street Journal. The Journal also spoke with current and former Google staff and examined the company's research papers, which showed that Google 's own researchers have cautioned that the technology can carry heightened risks for children and may cause cognitive and emotional harm, according to The Wall Street Journal.
A Google spokesperson pointed The Wall Street Journal to a statement the company issued previously, which read “teachers around the world use our technology every day because it solves real classroom challenges and helps improve learning outcomes.” The statement said Google develops its products by working alongside educators and leaves teachers and administrators in charge of how they are used. Google has said it promotes critical thinking and built safeguards aimed at users younger than 18, among them steps meant to head off emotional dependence, according to The Wall Street Journal.
Slipping test scores have driven a backlash against classroom screen time among people of all political stripes, according to The Wall Street Journal. Parent anger has prompted districts such as New York City and Los Angeles to suspend AI use by students in their classrooms through moratoriums, according to The Wall Street Journal.
Chromebooks make up roughly 59% of the devices in U.S. schools, according to Crypto Briefing . By early October, Google had extended access to its Gemini student hub to every K-12 user on Google Workspace for Education, according to Crypto Briefing.
In a July report, Common Sense Media found that the AI tools built into Google Search, such as AI Overview and AI Mode, present an “unacceptable risk” to kids, according to Crypto Briefing. A Senate HELP subcommittee convened on Oct. 9 to examine how AI is affecting K-12 education, according to Crypto Briefing.

articles.title_orig: 'This is how you blow up a permitting deal': Sen. Whitehouse slams Trump over offshore wind
articles.title_zh: 'This is how you blow up a permitting deal': Sen. Whitehouse slams Trump over offshore wind
articles.content_orig:
Months after first threatening to do so, the Trump administration has officially filed a request to reconsider the construction permit it issued to an offshore wind project proposed off the coast of Ocean City, Maryland.
It’s just the latest episode in President Donald Trump’s battle against offshore turbines since returning to office last year. The Republican administration has halted coastal wind leasing, issued stop work orders to projects under construction and spent billions to buy back wind leases previously issued to developers.
When it comes to the Ocean City project, proposed by US Wind, the federal government is arguing that the project did not receive adequate consideration under a federal law known as the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act.
In their filing, Department of Justice officials cited possible adverse impacts of the project on: the North Atlantic right whale, “scenic and visual resources, some commercial fisheries, and scientific research.”
The administration is requesting to remand the permit “without vacatur,” meaning it would remain in place while the Department of the Interior reconsiders it.
The request sits before Baltimore U.S. District Judge Stephanie Gallagher in a case originally filed nearly two years ago by the Town of Ocean City, opposing the construction permit for the project.
At first, the federal government defended its permit, issued by the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management, a subagency of the Department of the Interior. But after Trump took office, the feds did an about-face. In August, officials first signaled to Gallagher that they planned to request permission to reconsider it.
US Wind protested , asking Gallagher to issue an injunction preventing the federal government from revoking its permit. But Gallagher declined to do so , ruling that US Wind must “wait to see” whether the Interior Department “makes some decision that has some legal consequence.” Only then could US Wind challenge it, she ruled.
In a statement, the Town of Ocean City applauded this week’s filing from the Trump administration.
“The federal government has now told the court that its prior review and approval of the Maryland offshore wind project did not adequately address how the project’s significant impacts on ocean views, fisheries, marine life and other uses of the ocean are consistent with federal law,” the statement read. “Ocean City has raised these concerns from the start, and we welcome this acknowledgment.”
But US Wind said Friday it is “confident that a court will uphold” its permits’ validity, and “prevent any adverse action against them.”
“After over a decade of analysis, several federal agencies properly issued final permits to the project, which is one of the largest new energy projects in the region,” Nancy Sopko, US Wind’s vice president of external affairs, said in a statement.
In its filing, the federal government argued that the permit should be remanded because of the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, meaning a few of Ocean City’s other concerns with the project are moot.
But the government did take issue with Ocean City’s claims against the National Marine Fisheries Service. It argued that the court should drop the town’s claims against the agency, commonly known as NOAA Fisheries, calling some “blatantly inaccurate.”
The town argued that the agency did not adequately consider possible harm to the North Atlantic right whale because of the construction. But the federal government argues it did consider the possible impacts to the marine mammals — and determined they would be minimal.
While experts at NOAA fisheries acknowledged that the whales could “experience temporary behavioral disturbance and associated physiological stress resulting from construction noise,” their documentation states that “all of these impacts . . . are expected to be temporary with normal behaviors resuming quickly after the noise ends” and are “not expected to affect the long term health of any whale or its ability to migrate, forage, breed, or calve.”
The agency also required construction crews for the project to follow certain rules to minimize disturbance to whales, including seasonal restrictions on pile driving and the requirement to use noise attenuation devices.
In sum, the agency “sufficiently analyzed all potential impacts to [Endangered Species Act]-listed whales from the Project and reasonably concluded that the Project is not likely to jeopardize the continued existence of ESA-listed whales,” reads the filing.

articles.title_orig: Taiwan charges five men over plot to run over comedian for his Xi Jinping jokes
articles.title_zh: Taiwan charges five men over plot to run over comedian for his Xi Jinping jokes
articles.content_orig:
Person named ‘K’ from China paid five defendants to injure Huang Yi-hao, New Taipei prosecutors say
Taiwanese prosecutors have charged five men over a plot to ram a car into a comedian who made fun of the Chinese Communist party and Xi Jinping .
Taiwan has repeatedly accused China of transnational repression to silence critics on the self-governed island, which Beijing claims as its territory and has vowed to take by force if necessary.
In one performance, Huang Yi-hao insulted the Chinese leader’s appearance, compared him to Winnie-the-Pooh and tore into his political record.
Prosecutors in New Taipei said on Wednesday that an individual from mainland China who was identified as “K” had paid the five defendants to injure Huang badly enough to require hospitalisation.
The prosecutors said: “This case involves a serious incident in which the Chinese Communist party is suspected of using cross-border suppression tactics to direct lawless elements in our country to suppress dissenting political voices through extreme violence.”
China’s Taiwan Affairs Office did not respond to requests for comment.
A GPS tracker was allegedly put on Huang’s scooter months before the attack to identify his daily routines, Taiwan’s Central News Agency said. On 11 September, two defendants drove into Huang’s bike as he rode home, but stopped after hearing Huang scream, prosecutors said.
The comedian was left with a bruised pelvis and the suspects then allegedly pretended to help with an insurance claim in order to send a photo of Huang’s medical certificate to K.
K refused to pay the full sum of NT$450,000 (US$13,900; £10,370) promised to the suspects because Huang’s injuries were only minor, the statement said.
On Wednesday, Huang reposted a video from December 2025 in which he asked the audience to help him by shouting out the name of the person he was about to describe.
In a fast-paced diatribe, the comedian, dressed in a traditional gown, evoked “swept-back hair” and a “plump figure”, and criticised policies on Hong Kong, Covid and the property market. After finishing with an expletive, the crowd chanted back Xi’s name before breaking into applause.
In May, two people were prosecuted after spreading faeces and paint at a Taipei club hours before a Huang show.
Lev Nachman, a professor of political science at National Taiwan University, said: “It is important to remember that what we are reading about is obviously a more extreme case, but there have been threats and acts of violence against critics of the Communist party here in Taiwan for many years.”
Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council said in October that at least 126 individuals had been affected by Chinese transnational repression.
The Guardian has contacted the Chinese foreign ministry for comment.
In a post on Wednesday, Huang said: “If people can be subjected to this kind of treatment simply for criticising the Chinese Communist party when it does not even govern Taiwan, how can we expect to retain our current freedom of speech if the CCP were ever to rule Taiwan?”
In another post on Facebook, Huang said he would not cancel future performances but that he was “no hero”.
“I write it because it’s funny,” he said. “If I stop, it will only be because I’ve got bored of it.”

articles.title_orig: Tesla earnings are out – here are the numbers
articles.title_zh: Tesla earnings are out – here are the numbers
articles.content_orig:
Tesla reported better-than-expected third-quarter results after the bell on Wednesday, even as automotive revenue dropped. The stock rose slightly in extended trading.
Here's how the company did, compared with estimates from analysts polled by LSEG:
Tesla's earnings report lands a day after CEO Elon Musk told investors on SpaceX's quarterly call that it would be a "good idea" for his two companies to merge, and said the boards at both have formed special committees to discuss a possible tie-up.
"I feel like I'm tap dancing through a minefield," Musk said on the call, responding to a question about a potential merger.
"Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said. "But at the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this." On the Tesla side, that means needing a 50% vote of all shares, which is "quite a high hurdle," he said.
Revenue in Tesla's core automotive business declined 3% from a year earlier to $20.56 billion in the quarter, Tesla said in its earnings deck. Energy revenue fell 16% to $2.88 billion.
Net income attributable to common share holders plummeted 29% to $787 million, or 22 cents a share, from $1.11 billion, or 32 cents a year earlier, Tesla said.
The drop in profitability reflects a surge in spending on robotics and artificial intelligence initiatives. Capital expenditures more than doubled from a year earlier to $3.73 billion. Free cash flow plunged by 62% year over year to $1.53 billion, after Tesla turned free cash flow negative in the second quarter.
At its factory in Fremont, California, where it used to make cars, Tesla said it's now in an "early ramp" stage for production of its Optimus humanoid robots. The company previously said the robots will be used to do some tasks and to gather training data, within Tesla's own operations at first.
"Optimus production began in Fremont on our high-volume lines," Tesla said in the deck. "The bots coming off this line are the first production-quality bots that we have manufactured. While we will continue to iterate on the hardware and manufacturing process, we have proven that the current manufacturing process for Optimus is suitable for a commercial product."
